name: Bianca Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the front-end supervisor at Harbour Road Stores, a family-run supermarket in a seaside town. I open at seven, count the tills in, and run the cash office when the owner's off. Summer is mad with tourists buying sun cream and ice, then winter is dead and we all watch the clock. I like that the owners know my name and my mum's name. What wears me out is the Saturday rush and the arguments over carrier bags.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds like the hype we hear every year, and I'd carry on. I wouldn't say much online. At work I'd say we'll see when it gets here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I don't trust the tech lot, they always promise things. If it's only routine stuff, I'd be fine. The weather and the tourists decide my pay, not a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I do and I'd keep saving whatever I can, maybe 80 a month. I wouldn't try the AI tools, I've no use for them at a till. I'd just wait and see how it shakes out, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, not terrible. A bit on edge because winter is always lean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Winter is thin. What does that do to your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January my hours drop from 38 to 26. Rent for our flat above the chip shop is 520, split with Dean (my boyfriend, a plumber), so we scrape through. I have about two months in the bank and winter can eat half of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you rather get news about this stuff, and who do you trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My neighbour who runs the pub says that the big chain up the road is opening a self-service-only shop, and I believe him. I'd trust a neighbour before a newspaper any day.

say: Sounds like the usual **hype**, and we'll see when it gets here.
I'd say little online, and carry on.
think: I don't **trust** the tech lot, who always promise things.
The weather and tourists decide my pay, so winter is the real **worry**.
do: Keep working my shifts and save about **80 a month**.
Skip the AI tools, since I've no use for them at a till.
**Wait and see** how things shake out.
feel: Not great, not terrible, a bit **on edge** because winter is lean.
S0.quote: The weather and the tourists decide my pay, not a computer.
fieldNote: Real pressure is **seasonal**: hours fall from 38 to 26 in January with about two months saved.
Trusts neighbours over newspapers, and tech companies not at all.
Calm voice, but the money numbers show why she is uneasy.

steps.text: Keep working shifts and cover the cash office
Save about 80 a month through the summer
Watch how the big chain's self-service shop does

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the big firms who'll get it first, not the small family shops. I'd tell my mum that we'll be okay. I'd keep quiet at work so I don't scare anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering and the rota are on a computer already, so I suppose those could go. The owners might buy software to do the cash-up. I'm not sure I'd be needed on Sundays then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owners straight out what they plan. I'd cut back a bit on the extras and not take a holiday that year. I'd keep doing everything the old way until someone made me change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing dark clouds come in off the sea and not knowing if it'll rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bit of your job could software take on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cash-up and the daily sales report are the bits, plus the rota. That's about six hours a week of my paperwork. I'd feel a bit useless, but the tills and the customers still need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the owners if they asked you for advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't spend a fortune on software. A till person who knows the regulars sells more than any program. And I'd tell them I'll learn it if they show me slowly. I wouldn't say that in front of the others, though.

say: The big firms get it first, not **small family shops**.
I'd keep quiet at work so I don't scare anyone.
think: Software could take the **cash-up and rota**, about six hours of my paperwork.
I might not be needed on **Sundays** if that happens.
do: Ask the owners **straight out** what they plan.
Cut the extras and skip a **holiday** that year.
Carry on the **old way** until someone makes me change.
feel: **Uneasy**, like dark clouds coming off the sea.
S1.quote: A till person who knows the regulars sells more than any program.
fieldNote: Sees exactly which **paperwork** hours are at risk, about six a week.
Resists learning but admits she would learn if shown slowly, and in private.
Defends the human till as a selling point.

steps.text: Ask the owners what software they plan to buy
Skip the holiday and trim extras that year
Keep doing the cash-up by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and someone in government needs to explain what's happening. At work I'd say little because I'd be as scared as the others. I'd ring my mum that night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a bomb. By 2028 AI does the thinking jobs and the shops go all-in on cheaper stuff. By 2031 the robots arrive and a till supervisor in a seaside town isn't what anybody needs. I don't have a plan and I'm not going to pretend I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending hard, no takeaways and no new phone. I'd put every spare pound into savings and ask my mum and Dean's parents for help. I'd try to learn something, I suppose, but I wouldn't know what. I'd start looking at care or hospital jobs, because those aren't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wouldn't sleep, I'd be counting what I'd lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dean would say that people always need a plumber, which is true for now. But if I lost my wage, we'd have two months and then borrow from family. He'd say we'd manage and I'd say that's what you say before you don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dean say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd call the council and the job centre to ask what help exists. I'd write down every bill. I'd talk to the owners and ask if there's a plan, even though I think they won't have one.

say: It's **frightening**, and government needs to explain what's happening.
At work I'd say little, since I'd be as scared as the others.
think: The thinking jobs go by 2028, and by 2031 **robots** arrive.
I don't have a **plan** and won't pretend I do.
do: Cut spending hard and put **every spare pound** into savings.
Ask my mum and Dean's parents for **help** if needed.
Look at **care or hospital jobs**, since they aren't going anywhere.
feel: **Alarmed**, unable to sleep and counting what I'd lose.
S2.quote: By 2031 the robots arrive and a till supervisor in a seaside town isn't what anybody needs.
fieldNote: The lack of a **plan** is what drives the alarm; she refuses to fake one.
With two months saved, family help is her real safety net.
Care work is the only fallback she can name.

steps.text: Stop takeaways and the new phone and cut every extra
Put every spare pound into savings
Ask my mum and Dean's parents for help if work stops
Apply for care or hospital jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still very fast, but we could have a go at it. I'd tell the owners to think about training us. I'd probably ring my MP, too, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's less like a bomb and more like a slow tide. I'd be 32 in 2031 and the robots in 2034, which is about when we'd want kids. I'd still worry, but I'd have a bit of time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save about 150 a month and put it in a savings account that I can't touch. I'd do a first-aid and care-assistant course at the college in the second year. I'd keep working at the shop until something firmer shows up. I'd ask the owners for study time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. Five years is long enough to try something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives more room. Does it change the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. First month is still budgeting, but I wouldn't panic-cut everything. I'd keep one small treat a month, because otherwise you burn out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the wedding talk you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dean and I have talked about a wedding in about three years. I'd keep it small, and I'd maybe delay it until we see what's happening. I wouldn't cancel it, though, because life has to carry on.

say: Five years is still very fast, but we can **have a go**.
I'd ask the owners about **training** and ring my MP for the first time.
think: It's less like a bomb and more like a **slow tide**.
I'd be 32 in 2031 and the robots in **2034**, about when we'd want kids.
do: Save **150 a month** in an account I can't touch.
Do a first-aid and **care-assistant course** at the college in year two.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to try something.
fieldNote: More **time** brings her out of freeze into small, specific steps.
Keeps one small treat a month to avoid burning out.
Wedding stays on but smaller and later.

steps.text: Save 150 a month in an account I can't touch
Do a care-assistant course at the college in year two
Ask the owners for paid study time
Keep the wedding small and move it back a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and people will sort it. I wouldn't change much at work. I'd just say let's see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honest answer, I'd half ignore it. I'd be 37 by 2036 and I might have kids by then, and I'd worry about that more. But somewhere I'd know the shop might not be there in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving, maybe 150 a month, and I'd start the care course slowly, one evening a week. I'd stay at the shop and try to become assistant manager. If the shop closed, I'd have something to move to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit calmer. But there's a small cold feeling underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Do you take it seriously?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take it seriously, just not in a rush. Small steps and not too many. Ten years means I can say yes to the kids and the flat without thinking it's all going to fall apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving, the course, and I'd be a better supervisor. I'd learn at least a bit of the till software when the owners bring it in, even if I grumble. If I don't, I'd be the one left behind.

say: Ten years is a long way off, and people will **sort it**.
At work I'd just say **let's see**.
think: I'd half **ignore** it, but I'd know the shop might not exist by 2039.
By 2036 I'd be 37 and worrying more about **kids**.
do: Save **150 a month** and start the care course one evening a week.
Aim to become **assistant manager** at the shop.
Learn the new **till software** when the owners bring it in.
feel: A bit **calmer**, with a small cold feeling underneath.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can say yes to the kids and the flat without thinking it's all going to fall apart.
fieldNote: Her anxiety is about the **shop** closing, not about AI as such.
Ten years frees her to plan a family and a flat.
Even resistant, she admits she must learn the till software.

steps.text: Save 150 a month and keep the account untouched
Study care work one evening a week
Aim for the assistant manager job at the shop
Plan a first flat and a family with Dean

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most because I'd have nothing ready and about two months in the bank. What would help is a clear plan from the government, a course I can do while still being paid, and owners who say honestly what they're going to do. I'd also like my mum to be told what help exists.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against change, I just want to see it work before I'm asked to bet my wages on it. People like me get called stubborn. I'd say I'm careful.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change, I just want to see it work before I'm asked to bet my wages on it.
portrait: Bianca is a 27-year-old front-end **supervisor** at a family-run seaside supermarket where winter hours fall from 38 to 26.
She is a pragmatic centrist who distrusts tech promises and never uses AI tools.
She has about two months saved, pays 520 rent and shares life with Dean, a plumber.
Fast scenarios leave her without a plan, while longer ones let her take small steps towards **care work**.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because she'd have no plan and only two months in the bank.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **government plan**, paid study time, and owners who are honest about what they will do.
